Title: Exploring SYCL portability layer high-performance computing CPUs
Text:
Exploring SYCL as a portability layer for
high-performance computing on CPUs
Hari Abram
Chalmers University of Technology,
University of Gothenburg
Gothenburg, Sweden
hariv@chalmers.se
Nikela Papadopoulou
University of Glasgow
Glasgow, U.K.
nikela.papadopoulou@glasgow.ac.uk

University of Gothenburg
Gothenburg, Sweden
miquelp@chalmers.se
Abstract—As multicore vector processors improve in com-
putational and memory performance, running SIMT (Single
Instruction Multiple Threads) programs on CPUs has become
increasingly appealing, potentially eliminating the need for ded-
icated GPU hardware. SYCL is a royalty-free cross-platform
C++ programming model for heterogeneous computing that
implements the SIMT model and provides a path to run GPU
programs on CPU hardware. Several SYCL implementations
have been developed. To understand their performance on mul-
ticore vector CPUs, this paper systematically evaluates the two
major SYCL implementations using a set of micro-benchmarks
to assess key features such as memory bandwidth, kernel
scheduling, synchronization, and vectorization. We test SYCL
implementations across Intel Icelake, AMD Zen2, Fujitsu A64FX,
and AWS Graviton3 systems, comparing Ahead-of-Time (AoT)
and Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation flows, with OpenCL and
OpenMP backends, and compare the results with native OpenMP
implementations. Based on the results from these experiments,
we generate a table of recommendations for SYCL developers. In
general, our results show that AoT outperforms JIT in memory
bandwidth, while JIT excels in scheduling and synchronization.
SYCL on A64FX achieves near-peak memory bandwidth but
underperforms in parallelization and reduction tasks. Our study
also explores data management strategies, including USM and
buffer & accessor (B&A), and backend configurations, revealing
that these factors significantly impact performance. Our findings
underscore the importance of selecting the appropriate toolchain
to maximize SYCL’s potential for portable and high-performance
execution across diverse hardware platforms.
Index Terms—Benchmarking, CPUs, SYCL, OpenMP, Intel
OneAPI, DPC++, AdaptiveCpp
I. INTRODUCTION
Recent advances in heterogeneous architectures have raised
concerns about performance portability and the complexity
of application porting. To address these, the Khronos Group
developed the SYCL standard [1], which aims to target perfor-
mance portability across different architectures. SYCL follows
an SPMD (single-program, multiple-data) approach similar
to OpenCL/CUDA and is primarily designed for GPU-based
computing. However, current trends in CPU architectures, such
as long vector widths and high memory bandwidth exemplified
by processors like the Fujitsu A64FX, are being explored to
achieve performance levels comparable to those of GPUs [2]–
[6]. These developments underscore the need to analyze the
performance of SYCL on CPUs.
The open nature of SYCL allows for various implemen-
tations, each relying on different compilation toolchains and
runtimes. When targeting CPUs, Intel DPC++ [7] employs
JIT compilation with an OpenCL backend. At the same
time, AdaptiveCpp [8] can employ either JIT compilation,
with OpenCL or OpenMP runtime, or AoT(Ahead-Of-Time)
compilation with OpenMP. This differs from GPU-targeted
SYCL, which typically relies on vendor-provided runtime
systems, such as CUDA with NVIDIA GPUs. Achieving
peak performance when executing SYCL code on CPUs is
challenging due to the wide variety of available runtimes and
compilation methods. This raises the critical question of which
toolchain should be selected when targeting specific CPUs.
SYCL can act as a portability layer across GPUs and CPUs,
but its performance on multicore vector CPUs needs careful
evaluation. Inheriting its design from OpenCL, SYCL is
more closely aligned with GPU-like architectures. Therefore,
its effectiveness on modern CPUs requires further investiga-
tion and analysis. SYCL offers multiple ways to parallelize
a kernel offloaded to a runtime, such as utilizing various
iteration spaces (sycl::range vs sycl::nd_range),
dimensions, and data management methods (USM (Unified
Shared Memory) vs B&A (Buffer and Accessors)). Combining
these diverse methods with the various toolchains available
in SYCL implementations presents a challenge for developers
aiming to achieve acceptable performance in their applications,
considering these methods were developed to target GPU-like
architectures. Motivation: Given the diverse array of toolchains
available for targeting CPUs through SYCL, how can we
effectively leverage these toolchains to optimize performance
on multicore vector CPUs? This paper characterizes the per-
formance of SYCL methods, focusing on the impact of these
methods on vectorization, scheduling, and synchronization.
Quantifying the influence of runtimes and compilation flows
on the performance of SYCL features through application-
level benchmarks is challenging due to the difficulty of achiev-
ing isolation across SYCL features, given the interplay of the
various SYCL features used in such benchmarks. Additionally,
although similar analyses have been conducted on specific
applications [9]–[17], it remains challenging to pinpoint the
specific SYCL features that contribute to performance bottle-
necks. To address this, we have developed a suite of micro-


benchmarks1 that enable a bottom-up approach for assessing
the performance of SYCL features across various imple-
mentations and runtimes on CPUs. These micro-benchmarks
complement existing SYCL benchmark suites such as SYCL-
Bench [18], HeCBench [19] and PRK [20], by enhancing the
scope and depth of the benchmarks. We achieve this through
the use of different methodologies and by incorporating more
parametrization, allowing for a more comprehensive evaluation
of SYCL performance across various configurations.
Our microbenchmarks evaluate the impact of runtime on
memory bandwidth, parallelization, vectorization, and other
factors on four processors with different ISAs: Intel Icelake,
AMD Zen2, Fujitsu A64FX, and AWS Graviton3. These four
processors are selected to showcase different vectorization
and parallelization capabilities. We also compare the perfor-
mance of SYCL against OpenMP by developing equivalent
OpenMP benchmarks, which serve as our baseline, consider-
ing OpenMP is a standard parallel programming model for
CPUs. Note that, unlike SYCL, OpenMP requires specific
constructs to address GPUs, compared to the standard method
when targeting CPUs, this requires an extra effort to make
OpenMP single-source portable, though this effort may be
minimal. Our analysis aims to identify key SYCL features and
the impact of runtime and backend choices on performance,to
achieve portable and acceptable performance across systems.
With our microbenchmarks, we observe the performance
difference across SYCL implementation versions, compilation
flows and backends while testing for performance portability
across systems. Specifically, we observe that JIT with OpenCL
is preferred when data movement between main memory and
the processor is minimal, whereas AoT with OpenMP is
preferred when there is a need for high memory bandwidth.
In addition, we show that SYCL on x86 machines outper-
forms AArch64 systems in scheduling and synchronization
tasks. When SYCL is compared to OpenMP, performance
superiority varies by system and SYCL implementation, with
some JIT workflows outperforming OpenMP, particularly in
parallelization, where JIT compilation performs up to 10%
better than OpenMP. More detailed findings are presented
in Table VIII. Overall, our experiments suggest that SYCL
performance on multi-core vector CPUs is influenced by
factors such as compilation flows, backend choice, and system-
specific hardware features.
This paper makes the following contributions:
• We systematically evaluate the various runtimes and
compilation flow toolchains of SYCL implementations
when targeting modern multicore CPUs with vectoriza-
tion capabilities.
• We assess the potential of SYCL for portability across
different CPU architectures by evaluating its utilization
of available features on various hardware platforms.
• We show that the achieved memory bandwidth is strongly
influenced by the compilation flow, with AoT compila-
tion achieving the highest possible bandwidth across all

mance with JIT compilation. Additionally, our findings

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We
discuss related work in Section II. Section III outlines our
SYCL micro-benchmarks. Section IV provides details on the
experimental configuration. In Section V, we present our
experimental results for the developed micro-benchmarks and
discuss our findings. We conclude this work in Section VI.
II. RELATED WORK
With the rising popularity of SYCL, several works have used
SYCL as the programming model of their choice [9]–[16],
which has led to the development of several SYCL benchmark
suites [18], [20]–[22]. The SYCL-Bench suite [18], [21] offers
valuable insights into the performance of SYCL. It has certain
similarities to our work, particularly in trying to characterize
the SYCL runtime effects, focusing on task scheduling and
data management. However, the primary target of this research
work is GPUs, with benchmarks specifically designed to
characterize GPU runtimes and architectures. Our work aims
to target multicore vector-capable CPUs by focusing on the
specific aspects of SYCL performance. Still, the main reason
for developing our microbenchmarks rather than using SYCL-
bench is due to the degree of freedom available and the
in-depth analysis we can achieve, compared to using other
benchmark suites. For example, in SYCL-bench, each kernel is
predominantly executed using a single method, whereas, in our
micro-benchmark suite, we test multiple methods to initiate the
execution of kernel for each of the micro-benchmarks.
Several research works also have benchmark suites to
assess SYCL performance in the heterogeneous landscape.
The PRK benchmarks [20], [22] comprise three benchmarks
implemented in SYCL: stream, 2D stencil, and point-to-point
synchronization. While these benchmarks are useful, they
have limitations in fully characterizing SYCL implementations
and their runtime behavior. The Rodinia Benchmarks [17]
have also been ported to SYCL. The complexity of these
benchmarks imposes constraints on characterizing the runtime
effects of SYCL features. Moreover, the intricacy makes
it challenging to study the effects of SYCL constructs in
isolation. HeCBench [19] has been developed to test the
performance portability of SYCL at the application level.
These three benchmark suites are primarily designed to test
the SYCL performance at the application level.
Recent work by [23] investigates the offloading of the kernel
matrix assembly in PLSSVM (Parallel Least Squares Support
Vector Machine) using various SYCL methods. This research
shares a similar objective to our study, but differs in its
approach to analyzing performance overheads. While the paper
focus on the overall performance of kernels in different kernel
offloading methods, our study measures the overheads incurred
during the scheduling of parallel tasks using various offloading
methods. This allows us to analyze task scheduling overhead
independently, without the influence of kernel computation


overhead. Several research works have predominantly focused
on the process of porting applications to SYCL, documenting
the experiences and challenges encountered. Examples of
previous research work with SYCL include the conjugate
gradient [9], molecular dynamics applications [12], stellar
merges simulations [13], epistasis detection [14], LU decom-
position [15], cluster methods [10], bandwidth-bound applica-
tions [24], Fourier transform library [16] and AI graphs [11].
In recent work, Joube et al. [25] implement diverse memory
management strategies within SYCL to evaluate their effec-
tiveness, this approach aims to provide a more comprehensive
understanding of the intricacies surrounding the performance
implications of employing these features in SYCL-based ap-
plications.
III. METHODOLOGY
This work focuses primarily on the performance charac-
terization of various SYCL features through the utilization
of microbenchmarks. To effectively understand the impact of
compilation toolchains and runtimes on the various param-
eters through which SYCL kernels are executed on CPUs,
flexibility and parametrization are essential when offloading
these microkernels. This need for flexibility led to the devel-
opment of our suite of microbenchmarks. The inspiration for
this approach comes from the EPCC benchmark suite [26],
a well-established collection of OpenMP microbenchmarks
designed to evaluate the performance of parallel constructs
and features in OpenMP. Within our micro-benchmark suite,
we analyze a range of SYCL features, including memory
bandwidth of Unified Shared Memory (USM) allocations,
parallel constructs employing range and nd_range objects,
various SYCL data management techniques, accumulation via
atomic operations, reduction, as well as group and subgroup
barriers. Additionally, our suite includes microbenchmarks to
evaluate the impact of vectorization on SYCL kernels, when
various SYCL features are combined. Each microbenchmark is
executed 100 times, with the resulting average, median, max-
imum, and minimum execution times used for performance
comparison. It is important to note that all variables considered
in this micro-benchmark study are of type double. Although
the experiments were also conducted using the float type,
similar trends were observed for both types.
In the following subsections, we provide detailed descrip-
tions of each of these features and the corresponding mi-
crobenchmarks that we have developed for their evaluation.
Furthermore, we outline our definition of the baseline per-
formance for each feature, also explaining how we obtain
the baseline, to effectively measure any additional overhead
introduced by the SYCL software stack.
A. Microbenchmarks for Evaluating SYCL Features
1) Memory bandwidth: The SYCL standard encompasses
three distinct methods for USM data allocation, namely,
sycl::malloc_host,
sycl::malloc_shared,
and
sycl::malloc_device. The first method allocates shared
data and pins it to the host memory, facilitating access by both
the host and the device, while the second method allocates
a shared memory region that is similarly accessible by both
the host and the device, but pins it to the device. The third
method allocates device-specific memory, which can only
be accessed by the device, and is pinned to the device.
In our microbenchmark, we evaluate the memory bandwidth
observed when employing these different memory allocation
methods. Furthermore, we examine the memory bandwidth
performance when using the range and nd_range iteration
spaces. These different data management strategies in SYCL
are used to target heterogeneous computing systems, where
data has to be transferred from CPU to accelerator or GPU,
it is important to note that since the experiments within our
work execute their kernels on a CPU, the host and device
are equivalent from the implementation perspective. We then
compare this memory bandwidth with the bandwidth achieved
with the BabelStream [27] benchmark, which uses OpenMP
for parallelization.
2) Parallelization: The parallel_for method is a prin-
cipal parallelization construct in SYCL that serves as the
means to delegate computational tasks to the device. It ac-
cepts two key inputs: a kernel, represented in the form of a
lambda function, and the iteration space defined using range
and nd_range objects. The method proceeds to generate a
distinct kernel instance for every iteration within the specified
iteration space, where the kernel instance corresponds to the
lambda function that is executed on individual threads created
by the runtime.
Kernel instances generated with the range template are
entirely independent of each other, and there is no commu-
nication or synchronization between these distinct instances.
On the other hand, the nd_range class template introduces
a concept of global and local range. The global range is
subdivided into subgroups defined by the local range. Ker-
nel instances associated with the local range possess shared
memory, facilitating communication and synchronization of
computation among these specific instances.
SYCL offers two distinct methods for offloading a kernel
to a device, depending on the data management strategy.
The first method involves the use of buffers and accessors,
where data is initially transferred to a sycl::buffer and
subsequently accessed through a sycl::accessor within
the sycl::handler. The second approach involves Uni-
fied Shared Memory (USM); here, global variables created
through the SYCL shared context can be accessed within
the sycl::handler, unlike variables created with general
memory allocations. The general approach to offloading a
kernel is demonstrated in Listing 1.
The microbenchmark designed for this feature assesses
the synchronization and scheduling overheads of the SYCL
backend runtime. This evaluation encompasses a range of
iteration spaces, each characterized by varying dimensions.
Furthermore, the benchmark serves to explore the influence of
both the problem size and the iteration space dimensions on
performance. These parameters are determined when declaring
a range or nd_range type, denoted as range<dim>.

3) Atomics and Reduction: To assess the performance of

4) Barriers: In the SYCL programming model, barriers can
be performed at the group level or the subgroup level. In
our microbenchmark, we evaluate these two different barriers,
both with USM and with buffer and accessors, but also with
different dimensions. We compare the performance of these
barriers with the OpenMP barriers.
B. Vectorization
This study extends its analysis to examine the vectorization
capabilities of the various SYCL implementations across dif-
ferent machines. Additionally, we investigate the compiler’s
auto-vectorization capabilities when using different iteration


spaces, such as sycl::range and sycl::nd_range, and
assess the effectiveness of employing different data manage-
ment strategies. The aim is to gain comprehensive insights into
how these factors impact the overall auto-vectorization perfor-
mance of SYCL implementations across different hardware
and SYCL constructs.
To thoroughly assess the vectorization properties, we intro-
duce four microbenchmarks in our set: GEMM (general matrix
multiplication), GEMV(general matrix-vector multiplication),
outer product, and cross-product. In these microbenchmarks,
we focus on evaluating the auto-vectorization capabilities of
SYCL implementations. The outer product benchmark an-
alyzes vectorization across work items, while the GEMM
kernel focuses on the vectorization of loops within work items
for a 2-dimensional iteration space. Similarly, GEMV tests
vectorization for a 1-dimensional iteration space. Additionally,
we include a cross-product kernel that implements conditionals
inside the kernel to analyze their impact on vectorization.

It is essential to highlight that all arrays and pointers are
initialized with the __restrict__ keyword. This keyword
serves as an indication to the compiler that the memory
locations of these arrays are independent, which is a critical
consideration for the accurate evaluation of auto-vectorization
properties. In the vectorization tests, we consider a benchmark
to be vectorized if the vector instruction counters show that
all cores have executed vector instructions and that the counts
are comparable to the average number of vector instructions
executed, calculated across all cores. This ensures that the
observed vectorization is not a result of computations unrelated
to the offloaded kernel but instead has a meaningful impact
on performance. We also analyze the compiler reports with
-Rpass-analysis flags, for a more thorough summary of
auto-vectorization. While reporting vectorization results, we
focus on whether the systems execute vector instructions and
the type of vector instructions.
IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
This work focuses primarily on assessing the performance
of SYCL features when executed on CPUs. To this end, we
select four CPUs for our experiments, an Intel Xeon Platinum
8358, an AMD EPYC™7742, a Fujitsu A64FX, and an
AWS Graviton3. We present the details of the experimental
platforms in Table I.
In this study, we use two distinct SYCL implementa-
tions, namely AdaptiveCpp and DPC++. Table II provides
an overview of the SYCL implementations with different
compilation flows and backends. Notably, the AdaptiveCpp
implementation is available with two different compilation
flows, JIT compilation and AoT compilation, each with dis-
tinct backends.
Table III presents the list of experiments conducted in this
study, which were carefully selected from a larger exploration
space. In the following paragraphs, we will briefly explain the
setup and tools used for each experiment.
To analyze historical performance trends, we opt to use sta-
ble versions of each SYCL implementation from 2022, 2023,
and 2024, conducting the comparison on x86 machines. For
older versions (v2022) of AdaptiveCpp, we had to use LLVM

We analyze the overheads associated with different compi-
lation workflows and backends on a single system, specifically
an Intel Xeon Platinum machine based on the Icelake microar-
chitecture. For this analysis, we utilize the latest versions of
AdaptiveCpp, compiled with LLVM v18.1.8.
To compare SYCL performance across different machines,
we utilize AdaptiveCpp, as this implementation functions
seamlessly across all the systems. On Fujitsu A64FX, it
has been shown in the Fujitsu compiler package documen-
tation [29] that the XOS MMM L PAGING POLICY en-
vironment variable has a significant impact on C++ code
performance on A64FX. However, this variable affects only
the Fujitsu compilers, which are not employed by any of
the SYCL implementations. We therefore do not set this
environment variable in our experiments.
We use LLVM to compile OpenMP code, which uses the
respective LLVM OpenMP runtime with v18.1.8. In all exper-
iments, we set the environment variable OMP_PROC_BIND
to true, as this results in better performance for both the
AdaptiveCpp (when offloaded to the OpenMP runtime) and
OpenMP code.
It is important to acknowledge that the systems examined
in this study feature different numbers of cores per node. In
our work, we restrict our experiments to the physical cores
and do not utilize Simultaneous Multi-Threading (SMT).
V. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
Our analysis systematically compares the experimental re-
sults obtained with various SYCL implementations, consider-
ing that these implementations may leverage different compi-
lation flows and backend runtimes.
Our evaluation assesses the performance of SYCL features
in relation to their dependency on the backend runtimes. We
evaluate each micro-benchmark with a range of problem sizes,
to determine whether the performance indicators scale with
increasing problem sizes. The term ”problem size” varies for
each micro-benchmark and may refer to parameters such as
array size, the number of instances of the kernel executed,
or a combination of both. We compare the different SYCL
versions and implementations in terms of execution time.
To compare with OpenMP, we normalize the SYCL results
against the OpenMP results. We omitted confidence intervals,
as the difference between mean, min and max is insignificant.
On average, we see a difference of < 1%, < 5% and <
1% between min, max and median, compared to the mean,
respectively, across benchmarks.
In the following subsections, we first present the historical
comparison of the AdaptiveCpp and DPC++ on x86 machines.
Next, we compare different backends with AdaptiveCpp on a
single machine. Subsequently, we evaluate the performance of
AdaptiveCpp on different machines. Finally, we examine the
vectorization properties of the various SYCL implementations
and backends.

B. Backend Comparison
Comparing different backends used for offloading SYCL
kernels provides insights into the overheads associated with
each backend and compilation flow. Since AdaptiveCpp can
offload to various backends via its generic JIT compilation
flow, we utilized AdaptiveCpp to perform a backend compar-
ison on the Intel Icelake machine. In Figures 4, 5, 6, 7, JIT
ocl and JIT omp correspond to Just-In-Time compiled SYCL
code offloaded to OpenCL and OpenMP respectively, and
similarly, AoT omp, corresponds to Ahead-of-Time compiled
SYCL code offloaded to OpenMP.
Figure 4 presents the memory bandwidth results for the
various backends and compilation flows when the memory
operations are performed on shared memory variables. We
observe that the AoT compilation flow with the OpenMP
backend achieves the highest bandwidth among the different
backends compared. When comparing the bandwidth obtained
by DPC++ with the OpenCL backend in Figure 1 to that
of the generic OpenCL backend of AdaptiveCpp, the results
are similar. This suggests that the OpenCL backend incurs
significant overhead during memory operations.
Through memory counters in LIKWID, we observe that
with JIT ocl, the TLB load and store misses were 3 and 3.7
times higher, and total loads and stores 13 and 15 times higher,
respectively, compared to AoT omp. Similarly, cycle stalls due
to memory operations during the execution of JIT ocl code
were 18.5 times higher than those observed with AoT omp
code. Although these findings suggest potential reasons for


the differences between JIT ocl and AoT omp, no such stark
contrasts were observed between JIT omp and AoT omp. This
indicates that the memory model used in OpenCL [30] may be
a key factor contributing to the poorer performance observed
with JIT ocl and AoT omp.

all systems, except Graviton3. However, the ability to vec-
torize conditionals within work items differs between x86
and AArch64 systems, with x86 machines demonstrating the
capability to vectorize conditionals effectively.
VI. CONCLUSION
In this work, we have developed a set of micro-benchmarks
to study the performance of various SYCL features on avail-
able toolchains and compilation flows of SYCL implemen-
tations. Furthermore, we analyze the performance overheads
of these SYCL features over standard programming models,
such as OpenMP. Our benchmarks test memory bandwidth,
parallelization, synchronization, and vectorization. We evalu-
ated two different SYCL implementations, AdaptiveCpp and
DPC++, on four different platforms: Intel Icelake, AMD
EPYC Zen2, Fujitsu A64FX, and AWS Graviton3.
Our experimental results demonstrate that different compi-
lation flows offer advantages in distinct aspects of the SYCL
programming model. Specifically, Ahead-Of-Time (AoT)
compilation is more effective for achieving higher memory
bandwidth, while Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation performs bet-
ter in parallelization tasks. Comparing different backends, we
observe similar trends. Across systems, SYCL on the A64FX
processor exhibits generally poor performance, while other
systems perform comparably to each other. The vectorization
benchmarks reveal that auto-vectorization depends heavily


on the sophistication of the compiler and its cost model.
Specifically, we observe that on the Graviton3 system, the
compiler struggles with auto-vectorization, indicating a lack
of optimization for vectorized instructions on this architecture.
For future work, we plan to integrate our benchmarks with
SYCL-Bench to complement the existing benchmark suite. We
also intend to conduct a more detailed study on vectorization,
expanding on the initial findings in future research.

Abstract: As multicore vector processors improve in com- putational and memory performance, running SIMT (Single Instruction Multiple Threads) programs on CPUs has become increasingly appealing, potentially eliminating the need for ded- icated GPU hardware. SYCL is a royalty-free cross-platform C++ programming model for heterogeneous computing that implements the SIMT model and provides a path to run GPU programs on CPU hardware. Several SYCL implementations have been developed. To understand their performance on mul- ticore vector CPUs, this paper systematically evaluates the two major SYCL implementations using a set of micro-benchmarks to assess key features such as memory bandwidth, kernel scheduling, synchronization, and vectorization. We test SYCL implementations across Intel Icelake, AMD Zen2, Fujitsu A64FX, and AWS Graviton3 systems, comparing Ahead-of-Time (AoT) and Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation flows, with OpenCL and OpenMP backends, and compare the results with native OpenMP implementations. Based on the results from these experiments, we generate a table of recommendations for SYCL developers. In general, our results show that AoT outperforms JIT in memory bandwidth, while JIT excels in scheduling and synchronization. SYCL on A64FX achieves near-peak memory bandwidth but underperforms in parallelization and reduction tasks. Our study also explores data management strategies, including USM and buffer & accessor (B&A), and backend configurations, revealing that these factors significantly impact performance. Our findings underscore the importance of selecting the appropriate toolchain to maximize SYCL’s potential for portable and high-performance execution across diverse hardware platforms.
